claim: RBF-HS returns the same diagnoses in the same best-first order as HS-Tree but in linear space, so savings do not cost soundness, completeness or order.
agent_test: none: guarantee is formal; test only that an agent's top-k suspect list under a token cap matches the unbounded list

claim: Under minimum-cardinality-first on 14 ontologies, RBF-HS saved memory by an average factor of 14.1 (ENT) and 13.8 (SPL), up to 57, with positive space-time tradeoff in 94% of non-trivial cases.
agent_test: Rerun best-first fault enumeration with a bounded frontier vs unbounded; compare tokens and rank of true fault

claim: Under most-probable-first, RBF-HS trades memory for time about one to one (median 3.75x less space, 3.56x more time; positive in 53% of cases); hours vs minutes at 100 diagnoses. The result for one preference criterion does not transfer to the other.
agent_test: Compare bounded vs unbounded frontier when candidate scores are nearly tied; expect re-expansion cost

claim: A hybrid (run HS-Tree for 400 nodes, then switch to RBF-HS) removes most RBF-HS time overhead (median 0-3%) with memory capped at 416 nodes versus over 500,000.
agent_test: Start with a cheap full frontier, switch to bounded re-exploration when the context budget fills

claim: Reusing the hitting-set tree across sequential diagnosis steps (DynamicHS) beats rebuilding: faster in 99.4% of scenarios and 96% of sessions, median saving 52%, max 75%; hardest cases median 64%, max 89%.
agent_test: Agent keeps its candidate-fault set between observations versus regenerating it; equal token budget

claim: DynamicHS is not free: it uses more memory (under twice HS-Tree in 82% of scenarios) and loses in a few scenarios (median -2% to -3%, single sessions up to 86% worse).
agent_test: Check persistence benefit shrinks when each new observation invalidates most candidates

claim: Finding several conflicts per call (MergeXplain) and parallel tree expansion speed up diagnosis; gains depend on conflict position, check cost and size (MergeXplain 20-30% random, up to 75% clustered, some negative cells; parallel 1.78-3.44x on 4 threads).
agent_test: Batch several independent consistency checks per model call instead of one; compare tokens

claim: Computing diagnoses directly, without conflict sets, helps when conflicts are hard to get: on 146 faulty OAEI-2011 alignments, HS-Tree could not return all requested leading diagnoses within 2 hours in 13 cases where the direct INV-HS-Tree could; timings elsewhere are mixed. Direct encodings are reported to beat HS-Tree when only one diagnosis is needed (FastDiag: about log2 consistency checks).
agent_test: For one-fault tasks use a direct divide-and-conquer probe; for multiple-fault tasks use conflict plus hitting set
audit_note: In the 13 cases HS-Tree within 2 hours could not return all the requested (1, 9, 30) leading diagnoses, but it did return 1 for csa-ekaw and 1 and 9 for ldoa-confof, so 'diagnosable only by the direct method' is too strong; 133/146 and mixed timings and FastDiag log2 checks are verified.
claim_before_audit: Computing diagnoses directly, without conflict sets, is needed when conflicts are hard to get: 13 of 146 faulty OAEI alignments were diagnosable only by the direct method; timings elsewhere are mixed. Direct encodings beat HS-Tree when only one diagnosis is needed (FastDiag: about log2 checks).

claim: Implicit hitting sets make multi-observation diagnosis scale: all 1140 buggy-encoder instances solved (largest about 0.1 s) while separate per-observation enumeration finished only 177 or 185.
agent_test: Diagnose with all failing observations jointly versus one at a time on a multi-failure task

claim: Sample choice for choosing the next measurement matters: random samples estimate elimination rate best, best-first samples estimate probability best; heuristic choice matters (wrong heuristic costs avg 100%, max 250% extra effort; no universal best).
agent_test: Pick next probe by an information heuristic with random vs top-k candidate samples; count probes to isolation

claim: Query synthesis picks near-optimal next queries without enumerating a pool (above 99.999% of optimal in under 1 s, handles 80 diagnoses vs about 10 for pool-based).
agent_test: Let the agent generate the discriminating probe directly instead of ranking a pre-listed pool

claim: Query-based ontology debugging saved users effort versus manual debugging in one user study: manual overhead 37% time and 117% mouse clicks, no loss in effectiveness.
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM directly

claim: Abstract or randomised approximation can be faster at small cost: random QuickXplain diagnoses beat a solver on scheduling (better in under half the time); abstract spreadsheet models 1 to over 4 orders faster, matching exact accuracy in a third of cases.
agent_test: Compare cheap approximate model vs full simulation of the system at equal tokens

claim: Using an LLM as a noisy consistency oracle inside QuickXplain plus greedy hitting set raises recall of valid claims on VitaminC (e.g. Sonnet 4.5 0.617 to 0.957, Opus 4.6 0.574 to 0.968) and F1 (Opus 4.6 0.611 to 0.976); the gain is small on FEVER.
agent_test: Our agent: replace one-shot 'which claims are inconsistent' with localise-then-delete; compare recall at equal tokens
note: Gap search: tested only with one call per query, temperature 0, no repeats; noisy-oracle robustness untested (d01, d02).

claim: Direct all-at-once LLM judging over-prunes (high precision, low recall); chain-of-thought, decomposition, few-shot and self-consistency do not fix it (recall .547 to .684 for Sonnet 3.7 variants).
agent_test: Add the prompting variants to our baseline arm and check recall of kept claims
note: Gap search: appendix Table 5 shows self-consistency prompt lowered recall in 5 of 5 judges, QXR recall .975 to .995 (d03). Not an equal-token test.

claim: On RAG evidence (RAMDocs, N=30) QXR helps weaker models most (Qwen2.5 32B recall .839 to .998; Haiku 4.5 F1 .724 to .863) and slightly hurts Sonnet 4.5 F1 (.882 to .870).
agent_test: Apply per model tier; use localisation only for weaker or cheaper executors

claim: LLM-oracle localisation is costly in calls: pairwise checks would need 435 calls at N=30 and 4,950 at N=100; QuickXplain needs O(k log N) per conflict. Oracle noise and non-monotonicity break QuickXplain guarantees.
agent_test: Measure tokens per recovered conflict against one-shot judging
note: Gap search: no measured call or token counts for QXR in the paper, only an O(Q) bound (d04).

claim: In one agent-debugging study exact minimum hitting set and a greedy method gave identical results (12/12 supports; 9/12 planted-fault recovery), so a better solver added nothing when the verifier already encoded the answer.
agent_test: Do not invest in exact solvers; test greedy first

claim: No study was found that tests RBF-HS, DynamicHS or other efficient hitting-set algorithms with an LLM; the only LLM uses (QXR, agent debugging) use QuickXplain or small greedy hitting sets.
agent_test: A literature gap, not testable
note: Gap search: the RBF-HS citation list (4 citers) shows no independent replication and no LLM use; EC-MHS and Frontiers papers unopened (d14-d17). Search APIs rate-limited, so absence is weak.

claim: Equal-cost comparison of localise-then-delete against self-consistency or best-of-N has not been run. The only prompt-sensitivity test (self-consistency prompt) lowered recall for all 5 judges, but did not match token budgets.
agent_test: Run QXR, best-of-N with a verifier, and majority vote at the same total token budget on a 30-claim set; compare recall and F1

claim: QXR has not been tested with a noisy or non-monotone oracle, and the weighted hitting set and graded oracle fixes are only proposed by the authors.
agent_test: Flip oracle answers at rates 5, 10, 20 percent and measure recall loss with and without weights or re-query near the boundary

claim: Evidence that QXR-like localisation works on diagnosis tasks is indirect: QXR was tested on claim sets of about 30 only. For reasoning chains, LLMs find the first error poorly (GPT-4 52.87 on BIG-Bench Mistake; o1-mini 87.9 vs GPT-4o 61.9 on ProcessBench) but fixing a known error works, and backtracking still helps at about 65 percent location accuracy.
agent_test: Apply bisection localisation to wrong reasoning chains and compare first-error accuracy with ProcessBench-style direct judging

claim: LLM-verbalised confidence on QA-style tasks is overconfident and weak at separating right from wrong answers (GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7 percent, values mostly 80 to 100 percent), though for RLHF models verbalised probabilities cut expected calibration error by over 50 percent relative to token probabilities; by extension, LLM-supplied fault priors for entropy or best-first heuristics should be treated as untested and not relied on.
agent_test: Ask the agent for suspect probabilities; score calibration on known-fault cases; compare random vs prior-guided probing
audit_note: Numbers verified (Xiong GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7%, values mostly 80-100%, GPT-3/3.5/Vicuna ECE >0.377; Tian verbalised cuts ECE by over 50% relative), but both studies test QA/classification confidence, not fault-probability priors for diagnosis, so the closing 'should not rely on LLM fault priors' is an extrapolation.
claim_before_audit: LLM-verbalised confidence is overconfident and weak at ranking right from wrong (GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7 percent, 80 to 100 percent values), though verbalised probabilities beat token probabilities by over 50 percent relative ECE. An agent should not rely on LLM fault priors for entropy or best-first heuristics.

claim: No test exists of reusing a candidate set across observations (DynamicHS idea) for an LLM with a limited context window, or of the suspect-list length at which a bounded frontier matters. Only indirect support: long-context position effects at 20 documents (GPT-3.5-Turbo below closed-book 56.1 percent when the answer is in the middle).
agent_test: Vary suspect-list length from 5 to 100 and measure rank of the true fault, with and without carrying the list forward
